title: kingdoms of amalur: reckoning™
text: Ok after quite a few more hours invested in the game then when my first review was made I think Im going to take another pass at it. Once again cannot stress enough that steam needs a neutral button. First off this game was not designed with wsad in mind. Even on the lowest setting the camera jerks around like mad. I could also spend an entire review complaining about the fov but many people have already done it much better than I ever could. Second the ui is absolute garbage. No effort was made to change the game into something pc friendly so you can only use 4 spells/abilities at once, and they are mapped to the same radial. I play as a jack of all trades and have 9 abilities, however im only able to use 4 in combat. 4. Diablo 3 had a better skill system than this. And for some unfathomable reason the useless 12 slot radial menu only allows you to bind potions. Thats it. Im playing on hard and I have only ever had to use health potions, which you can use by pressing r already. Wanna switch your weapons and try a different play style mid combat? Sure! Just press start, select items, select weapons, scroll all the way through what can be up to 70 weapons (you will never carry this many but thats how many backpack slots you have at first), select the weapon you want and bind it to either your primary or secondary weapon slot. 5 steps to switch weapons. And trust me, you will be doing this alot. So yeah the simple task of switching weapons completely breaks what little flow of combat there already was. Moving on to design I honestly have no problem with either the combat or the art style. The combat is darksiders and the art style is wow. Nuff said I want to balance all these cons with some pros now so here goes. The game is huge. At my current play time i havent even made it across half the game map, and I still have yet to head to either of the dlc maps. Also EA apparently has most of the voice actors from bethesdas works at their beck and call. Barry Dennen is always a welcome addition to any game. And the story is... well its alright. I felt a little let down with the first 15 minutes of the the game building me up as this whole fateless resurrected badass with the power of a god and the ability to change destiny itself then be told to go find some flowers for some schmuck so he can fight off the local creatures (thats what Im here for damn it!). But the characters they bother to give personality are kind of memorable: the drunken circus preformer trying to keep his troop together despite his wife/co-leader leaving him, the leader of a band of mercinaries more concerned with keeping his hold and troops in presentable condition than completing jobs. The storybook maiden doomed to play the part of a tyrant forever trying to break the cycle and giving you the chance to help her all the while the people who sent you after her begging you to make her keep her role because its "How the story is supposed to end." It all adds up. So I leave you with this. If you can shoulder your way past the fact that its not even a port, just a complete copy of its console version than its worth checking out. Dont buy it at full price though. But then who does these days? P.s thank you Coraline Castell for suggesting widescreen fixer. However the fact that a game this large lacks something as basic as a changable fov kind of speaks for itself.

title: kingdoms of amalur: reckoning™
text: This review is certainly a review I should have wirtten long ago, but here we are now. This game is brilliant, and I loved every second of this expansive game. The design of this game (Which comes from the narritive mind of R.A Salvatore, and Oblivion's director) is an overarching theme that all life is dictated by a thread of fate when they are first created or born; and the protagonist cheating fate and forging a fate of his own that affects the fate of all. The concept is one I've really not seen before in a video game narritive, and it definitely soothes my ache for strong philosophy and writing in video games. The story seems to lack a bit though.. You do meet a few characters througout the story, but they feel more like pieces on a Chess board than breathing individual (Besides one you meet towards the end of the game's second act), but I enjoyed their presences when they were around. The art is great, I love all of it. It evokes many different vibes, and the environments are lovingly crafted, despite the way each area on the map is segmented out, giving a weird map design in an otherwise fluid game world. Klurikon will forever stand in my brain as a testiment to how much focus a narritive design can have on the impact to the world around the player, while still delivering tight gameplay and fantastic visuals. The gameplay of Amalur is very reminiscent of the Fable series, giving open variety to the player, and rewarding the player for switching up their moveset and exploring the way to game works. In combat, the player may have two weapons equipped at a time, free to select either with the press of a button; while magic spells are always available to use, and can be selected via the keyboard, while the UI shows any macro'd spells. Fighting enemies offers the players points towards their fate bar, which builds up and allows the player to trance into a state where they can unleash their true awesome power and deliver satisfying finishers to enemies for extra exp, which is a fun treat to watch and revieve; performing well in fights (eg. not taking damage, varying up attack combos) will earn the player more points for the bar. The DLC is a whole review in itself, as it offers dozens of hours of fresh, new content, so I'll leave this review concise enough. Amalur is a grandly underrated game (I presume due to lack of marketing during its release) and deserves full attention of the gaming audience, please give it a chance to play, you won't be let down-- Look at my face, would I lie?

text: This is a single player action RPG. (Kinda like Fable) Kingdoms of Amalur features five distinct regions and four playble races. Almain (Civilized Humans), the Dokkalfar (Dark Elves), the Ljosalfar (Light Elves), and the Varani (Nomadic Humans. The combat includes a 'Fate' system which allows the player to accumulate 'fate points' and enter Reckoning Mode. Which is a slow motion mode that allows you to quickly kill enemies and do brutal finishing moves. The world is very big and lots of side quest. No jumping which is kinda sad, (There is only predesignated spots to jump down from) but there is swimming and you can find some cool spots and side quests.  You have ability to buy homes and upgrade them (A lot like Fable) and you can communicate with , rob or kill NPCs. Which have their own consequences. In all this is a great Action RPG 9/10

title: kingdoms of amalur: reckoning™
text: Finally decided to uninstall this - tried to play this on-and-off but it doesn't hold my interest, the game is like a fancy sword that lives in a scabbard which blunts itself when it's drawn. + Big game, lots of side quests, lots of dialogue - Boring quests, boring characters, boring mobs, over level for main quest + Lots of loot, crafting with alchemy and smithing - Too little inventory space, over powered weapons make the game too easy + Lots of different locations - Very same-ish dungeons, with boring travel to each new location (sparse mobs placement) Dodge mechanic would have made this extremely easy game already too easy - except hit boxes and attack timings seem all wrong. You can roll out of the way but still get hit. But your gear will by mitigating so much damage that you can just tank everything even as a caster. One hit bosses totally possible because the side-quest will over level you. The game is 70% travelling, 20% mowing down boring enemies and 10% skipping mundane dialogue. If you want lots of mediocre content for cheap, this game is great on sale. Can't recommend though.

title: l.a. noire
text: Pay attention now Noire fans! If L.A. Confidential The Third Man Casablanca or likewise movie titles ring a bell, GET THIS GAME! Never have I seen or played a game that nails the classic Noire setting so perfectly than L.A. Noire! The increasingly darkening plot, the sometimes cheesy, often macho and CERTAINLY political incorrect dialogue, Noire character exposition, lighting with strong contrasts and shadows, just to name a few. Hardcore fans can even set colours to black and white! The really good voice-over and the approach on facial expressions as part of the gameplay help a lot to immerse yourself. Sadly it is strictly Hollywood Noire and not European Noire . The soundtrack and action cues suffer a little because of this, but it still kicks! If you already know the aforementioned three movies, you will see some similarities plot-wise, but it is still exciting! There are even some cases that seem very fresh right now, like for example. title: l.a. noire
text: I got this game on sale with all the dlc for some ridiculously low price. I've heard good things, and the concept intrigued me, so that's the ultimate reason I pulled the trigger. I haven't played any of Rockstar's games in years, and I've never really been a big fan, so I wasn't too sure I would even like it. My favorite games tend to be first person, stealth, shooting / rpg type games like Fallout 3 / NV, Oblivion / Skyrim, Deus Ex, and Dishonored. With all that said, I would absolutely recommend this game to anybodywho has glanced at this game and been the least bit intrigued. It has something in it for everybody. Good dialogue and voice acting, interesting story, challenging action sequences, driving, shooting, invistigating. There's a lot going on here, and the game does a great job of bringing it all together. I'm also a sucker for the past and history, so I loved that the game is set in post WWII Los Angeles. The clothing, architecture, technology is all from that era, so for me that was really cool and also helped with immersion into the storyline. There is also a surprising amount of content. The story is long, and there are a ton of side missions you can do. I stayed away from the side missions because I was more interested in the story, which is unusual for me. I tend to do most or all side missions in games before tackling the story. Again, I feel like that says a lot about the immersion here. I was genuinely caught up in the storyline, and wanted to see what would happen next. With that said, my only major gripe about the game is that it gets really repetitive. They threw a couple new mechanics in here and there to keep you on your toes a bit, but for the most part, you end up doing the same kinds of things over and over aaand over. Another thing is that there don't seem to be too many (if any) real consequences for doing things badly, or straight up wrong. When interrogating, for example, it doesn't really seem like it matters if you get no answers or all of the answers. Even with those gripes though, this game was great, and I'm glad I gave it a shot. There's so much content here. I feel like I way more than got my money's worth even half way through the game. Like I said, if this game intrigues you at all, you should definitely give it a try, especially if you get it on discount.
